## Directions {.unnumbered}

Please turn in your **.qmd** and **.html** file on Brightspace. Please use the same naming convention as previous labs: `lastname_firstinit_lab_04.qmd` and `lastname_firstinit_lab_04.html`.

[You can download the `.qmd` file for this lab here.](https://github.com/nwakim/PUBH_523_26F/blob/main/project/lastname_firstinit_lab_04.qmd)

The above link will take you to your **editing** file. **Please do not remove anything from this editing file!!** You will only add your code and work to this file.

## Purpose {.unnumbered}

In Lab 3, you built a categorical version of your composite score(s), a clean overall summary table, and a grouped summary comparing your composite score across the groups of your other main variable. This lab turns those summaries into the actual **visualizations** you'll use in your final project.

Your final project's one-page information sheet is built around three findings:

1. One main variable on its own
2. The relationship between your two main variables
3. One main variable alongside one additional variable (optional in this lab, for 1 extra point)

For Findings 2 and 3, you'll use the **categorical** version of your composite score (from Lab 3) rather than the raw numeric score. Category breakdowns like "33% described access as difficult" are easier for a general audience to take in at a glance than a mean and standard deviation.

This lab has you build one polished visualization for each of these. By the end of this lab, you should have 2-3 finished, publication-ready plots saved as image files, which you can use in your final project. Some of the `ggplot2` code here is more involved than what you've used before, so this lab walks through each new piece in more detail than usual.

### Import your saved data from Lab 3

Your Lab 3 `.rda` file holds two objects: your dataset `wbns_06_cat` and your table `summary_table_overall`. This lab only needs `wbns_06_cat`, so we use the `which` argument to tell [`import()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/17_Import_Export/Import_Export.html#/rio-package) to pull out just that one, the same way you did in Lab 3. (Your summary table stays saved in your Lab 3 file. You can bring it into your final project if you want a table of your composite score.)

1.  Find your Lab 3 `.rda` file in your `data_project/data_processed` folder and note its exact name.
2.  Import `wbns_06_cat`. Replace the file name with yours:

    ```{r}
    #| eval: false
    wbns_06_cat <- import(
      here("data_project", "data_processed", "wbns_data_lab_03_work.rda"),
      which = "wbns_06_cat"
    )
    ```

3.  Use [`dim()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/16_Piping/Piping.html#/two-types-of-pipes-you-might-see) to print the number of rows and columns of `wbns_06_cat`. The number of rows should match the end of Lab 3.
4.  **Check your categories for `NA`s.** Use [`tabyl()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/28_Data_summarization_tables/Data_summarization_tables.html#/what-does-tabyl-do) on each categorical composite score (the variable(s) ending in `_cat`). If you see an `NA` row, those respondents don't have a composite score, and they'd show up as their own "NA" bar in every plot. Remove them with [`drop_na()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/25_Missing_data_transformations/Missing_data_transformations.html#/drop_na-removing-missingness-from-all-variables-in-the-dataset-1) and save the result back into `wbns_06_cat`:

    ```{r}
    #| eval: false
    wbns_06_cat <- wbns_06_cat |>
      drop_na(ease_free_food_cat)
    ```

    Use your own `_cat` variable(s). If there's no `NA` row, skip the `drop_na()`.

### Plan your three findings

In the final project, we will present 2-3 findings. These findings will include a table or plot to demonstrate the data/relationship. Before writing any plotting code, decide what each of your findings will show and which variable(s) it needs. This is a planning step: there is no code required here!

- **Finding 1 (one main variable on its own):** Which one of your main variables will you visualize by itself? It should be a **categorical** variable. **We recommend your other main variable** (not your composite score), listed first in your project's tab. Your composite score's categories already appear in Finding 2, so showing them again in Finding 1 would tell your reader almost the same thing twice. Using your other main variable gives your poster three different facts.
- **Finding 2 (the relationship between your two main variables):** No decisions here! Your project's tab lists which variable goes where. The rule: the variable your question asks *about the effect of* goes on the **x-axis** (one bar per group), and the **outcome** goes in the **fill** (the colored segments). That way, each bar answers a question like "Among people with difficult access to free food, what percent are food insecure?", which is the question your project asks.
- **Finding 3, optional (one main variable + one additional variable):** If you're building this one, which additional variable will you use? It goes on the x-axis, and your categorical composite score goes in the fill. Pick a **categorical** additional variable with a few short categories. Avoid counts like `num_children` (too many bars) and variables with many long category names like `race_ethnicity` (the labels will overlap, and some groups will be very small).

### Finding 1: Create the dataframe

Before plotting, we summarize the data into percentages to make our display a little more polished for the audience. We'll build a small dataframe of counts and percentages using [`count()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/21_Data_transformation_rows/Data_transformation_rows.html#/sorting-datasets-using-arrange) and [`mutate()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/22_Data_transformation_columns/Data_transformation_columns.html#/mutate-transform-and-create-variables). Here's how the code works:

```{r}
#| eval: false

finding1_data <- wbns_06_cat |>
  count(<your_main_variable>) |>              # <1>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100)               # <2>

finding1_data
```
1. `count()` counts how many respondents fall into each category of your Finding 1 variable, storing the result in a new column called `n`.
2. `mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100)` divides each category's count by the total across *all* categories, turning `n` into a percentage. Since there's no grouping variable yet, `sum(n)` here is just the overall total.

**Your turn:**

1.  Copy the code above into your editing file.
2.  Replace `<your_main_variable>` with your Finding 1 variable from your plan (no `< >`).
3.  Run it, and save the result as `finding1_data`.
4.  **Check your work:** the `pct` column should add up to 100.

::: callout-important

:::

### Finding 1: Visualize one main variable

Using `finding1_data`, create a bar chart of your Finding 1 variable. We use [`geom_col()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_bar.html) instead of [`geom_bar()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/31_Data_viz_Basic_plotting/Data_viz_Basic_plotting.html#/example-4-barplot-of-self-rated-health) (Lesson 31) here, because we already calculated the percentages ourselves. `geom_col()` plots the y-values you give it directly, while `geom_bar()` would try to do its own internal counting. Here's how the code works:

```{r}
#| eval: false

finding1_plot <- ggplot(finding1_data, aes(x = <your_main_variable>, y = pct)) +
  geom_col() + #<1>
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct, 1), "%")), vjust = -0.5, #<2>
            size = 6, fontface = "bold") + #<2>
  scale_x_discrete(labels = ________) + #<3>
  scale_y_continuous(limits = ______) + #<4>
  labs(______) + #<5>
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) #<6>

finding1_plot #<7>
```
1. Check out the extra arguments in `geom_col()`! You can change the fill or the width of the bars (Lesson 31).
2. [`geom_text()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_text.html) adds the percentage labels above each bar. `vjust = -0.5` nudges the labels slightly above the top of the bar, and `paste0(round(pct, 1), "%")` rounds the percentage to one decimal place and adds a percent sign.
3. `scale_x_discrete(labels = ...)` lets you swap in reader-friendly labels for the x-axis *without changing your underlying data*. Give it `c("old" = "new", ...)`: the names on the left of each `=` must exactly match the categories in your data, and the names on the right are what the reader will actually see. **Only use it if your categories aren't already reader-friendly.** Otherwise, delete this line.
4. When we plot percentages, it is often a good idea to plot the y-axis from 0 to 100: `c(0, 100)`.
5. [`labs()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/32_Data_viz_Design_choices/Data_viz_Design_choices.html#/basic-labelling-using-labs-titles-and-axes) (Lesson 32) lets you add a title, x-axis label, and y-axis label: `labs(title = "...", x = "...", y = "...")`. Use plain-language labels rather than variable names or question codes.
6. We can adjust the theme and font size (Lesson 32)!
7. Now we can print the plot!

**Your turn:**

1.  Copy the code above into your editing file, and replace `<your_main_variable>` with your Finding 1 variable.
2.  Fill in each blank (`______`), one at a time. Run the code after each one so you can see what it changed. Check your project's tab below for whether you need the [`scale_x_discrete()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/scale_discrete.html) line.
3.  Print `finding1_plot` and look at it: would someone who has never seen your data understand it?

- **`ease_free_food_cat`:** its categories are already reader-friendly, so delete the `scale_x_discrete()` line.

### Finding 2: Create the dataframe

Unlike Finding 1, you now need percentages calculated *within* each group on your x-axis (e.g., among people with difficult access to free food, what percentage are food insecure?). This time, you'll add [`group_by()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/29_Data_summarization_groups/Data_summarization_groups.html#/group-by-a-variable-in-get_summary_stats) before you calculate `pct`. Here's how the code works:

```{r}
#| eval: false

finding2_data <- wbns_06_cat |>
  count(<your_x_variable>, <your_fill_variable>) |>   # <1>
  group_by(<your_x_variable>) |>                       # <2>
  mutate(pct = ______) |> #<3>
  ungroup() #<4>

finding2_data
```
1. [`count()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/21_Data_transformation_rows/Data_transformation_rows.html#/sorting-datasets-using-arrange) counts how many respondents fall into every *combination* of the two variables (e.g., "difficult access AND food insecure," "difficult access AND not food insecure," and so on), storing the result in a new column called `n`.
2. `group_by(<your_x_variable>)` tells the following [`mutate()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/22_Data_transformation_columns/Data_transformation_columns.html#/mutate-transform-and-create-variables) to calculate `sum(n)` *separately within each group on your x-axis*. You used `group_by()` with `get_summary_stats()` in Lesson 29; it works the same way with `mutate()`.
3. Calculate the percent of each category within its group. The formula is the same as Finding 1.
4. [`ungroup()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/group_by.html) is new: it removes the grouping from the dataframe. It's a good habit after any `group_by()` + `mutate()`.

**Your turn:**

1.  Copy the code above into your editing file.
2.  Replace `<your_x_variable>` (in **both** places) and `<your_fill_variable>` with the Finding 2 variables from your project's tab in the plan above. Make sure the x-axis variable is the one inside `group_by()`: that's what makes each bar add up to 100%.
3.  Fill in the `pct` formula.
4.  Run it, and save the result as `finding2_data`.
5.  **Check your work:** within each x-axis group, the `pct` values should add up to 100.

### Finding 2: Visualize the relationship between your two main variables

Using `finding2_data`, create a 100%-stacked bar chart: one bar per x-axis group, split into the categories of your fill variable. As in Finding 1, we use [`geom_col()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_bar.html), since you already calculated the percentages yourself. Here's how the code works:

```{r}
#| eval: false

finding2_plot <- ggplot(finding2_data,
  aes(
      x = <your_x_variable>,
      y = pct,
      fill = <your_fill_variable>
      )
  ) +
  geom_col() + #<1>
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct), "%")), #<2>
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), #<2>
            color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 4.5) + #<2>
  scale_fill_discrete(labels = ________) + #<3>
  labs(______) + #<4>
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) #<5>

finding2_plot #<6>
```
1. Mapping `fill = <your_fill_variable>` (in the [`ggplot()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/30_Data_viz_Intro_to_ggplot/Data_viz_Intro_to_ggplot.html#/basic-layers-of-ggplot2) line above) tells `geom_col()` to draw one segment per category, stacked on top of each other by default. This creates the 100%-stacked bar. Check out the extra arguments in `geom_col()` too, like `width`.
2. [`geom_text()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_text.html) places its labels at the same x/y position as the data by default, which for stacked bars means the *top* of each segment. `position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5)` moves each label to the vertical *center* of its own segment instead, so it doesn't look like it belongs to the segment above it. `paste0(round(pct), "%")` builds the label text from your calculated percentage.
3. [`scale_fill_discrete()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/scale_discrete.html) is new: it works exactly like [`scale_x_discrete()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/scale_discrete.html) from Finding 1, but relabels the **legend** instead of the x-axis. **Only use it if your fill categories aren't already reader-friendly.** Otherwise, delete this line. (If your x-axis categories need relabeling too, add a `scale_x_discrete()` line, the same way as Finding 1.)
4. Same as Finding 1: add a plain-language title, x-axis label, and y-axis label. Also add `fill = "..."` to label the legend (Lesson 32). Keep your title **descriptive, not causal**: describe what the plot shows ("Food insecurity by ease of access to free food"), not why ("Easy access reduces food insecurity").
5. Same as Finding 1: adjust the theme and font size if you'd like.
6. Print the plot!

**Your turn:**

1.  Copy the code above into your editing file, and replace `<your_x_variable>` and `<your_fill_variable>` with the same variables you used to make `finding2_data`.
2.  Fill in each blank, and run the code after each one. Check your project's tab below for whether you need the `scale_fill_discrete()` line.
3.  Print `finding2_plot`. Check that the segments in each bar add up to 100%, and that the legend lists your categories in a meaningful order (the order comes from your data, not from this code).

::: {.panel-tabset group="project"}
#### Project 1

Your fill variable, `food_insecure`, has the categories `"No"` and `"Yes"`, which would show up that way in the legend. Keep the `scale_fill_discrete()` line, and relabel them the same way you did for the x-axis in Finding 1.

#### Project 2

- `self_rated_health` already has reader-friendly categories, so delete the `scale_fill_discrete()` line.
- `self_rated_health` has five categories, so each bar has up to five segments. If a small segment's label overlaps its neighbor, try a smaller `size` in `geom_text()`, or save the plot taller in the export step.

#### Project 3

`mental_health_score_cat` already has reader-friendly categories, so delete the `scale_fill_discrete()` line.
:::

If your composite score doesn't split cleanly into a small number of meaningful categories, a boxplot of the raw numeric score ([`geom_boxplot()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/31_Data_viz_Basic_plotting/Data_viz_Basic_plotting.html#/example-2-one-continuous-one-categorical-variable-12), Lesson 31) is a reasonable alternative. Just be consistent about which form (categorical or continuous) you use across Findings 2 and 3.

**Write your takeaway.** Below your plot, write **one sentence** that compares the groups on your x-axis, with numbers from your plot. For example: *"[X]% of [people in one x-axis group] [description of a fill category], compared with [Y]% of [people in another group]."* Keep it descriptive, not causal: say what differs between the groups, not that one variable causes the other. If the groups look about the same, say that. That's a finding too!

### Finding 3 (optional): Create the dataframe

Finding 3 is **optional** in this lab, and worth **1 extra point**. If you skip it, leave these sections blank in your editing file.

Your additional variable goes on the x-axis, and your categorical composite score goes in the fill (see your project's tab in the plan above).

::: {.callout-caution}
Your additional variables weren't cleaned in Lab 2 the way your main variables were. They may still contain "Refused" or "Don't know" (as real categories), or `NA`s. Skipping the cleaning step can quietly distort your plot, with a "Refused" bar or an "NA" bar.
:::

1.  **Look at your variable.** Use [`tabyl()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/28_Data_summarization_tables/Data_summarization_tables.html#/what-does-tabyl-do) on your additional variable to see its categories, including any "Refused", "Don't know", or `NA`.
2.  **Turn non-answers into `NA`.** Use [`replace_with_na()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/25_Missing_data_transformations/Missing_data_transformations.html#/replace_with_na-replace-a-factor-level-with-na) (Lesson 25), the same way you did in Lab 2 Part A. Spell each category exactly as it appears in your `tabyl()` output.
3.  **Remove the `NA`s.** Use [`drop_na()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/25_Missing_data_transformations/Missing_data_transformations.html#/drop_na-removing-missingness-from-all-variables-in-the-dataset-1) with your additional variable.
4.  Save the result as `finding3_clean`, and use `tabyl()` again to check that only real answers are left. A "Refused" row with a count of 0 is fine: the category name is still listed, but no one is in it, and [`count()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/21_Data_transformation_rows/Data_transformation_rows.html#/sorting-datasets-using-arrange) will skip it.
5.  **Build the dataframe** from `finding3_clean`, using the Finding 2 code: your additional variable takes the place of `<your_x_variable>`, and your composite score's `_cat` variable takes the place of `<your_fill_variable>`. Save it as `finding3_data`.

::: callout-important
#### Task (optional, 1 extra point)

Clean your chosen additional variable with `replace_with_na()` and `drop_na()`, and save it as `finding3_clean`. Then use `count()`, [`group_by()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/29_Data_summarization_groups/Data_summarization_groups.html#/group-by-a-variable-in-get_summary_stats), [`mutate()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/22_Data_transformation_columns/Data_transformation_columns.html#/mutate-transform-and-create-variables), and [`ungroup()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/group_by.html) to build a dataframe of within-group percentages. Save it as a new object called `finding3_data`, and print it.
:::

### Export your visualizations

Save each of your finished plots as a `.png` file. These files will be used later in the final project! If you need to adjust the size and look of your plots, you will need to come back to this lab, modify them, and re-export them.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Before you export: check each plot

Go through this list for each plot. If anything is missing, go back and fix it before you save.

- [ ] The **title** describes what the plot shows, in plain language, and doesn't claim that one thing causes another.
- [ ] The **x-axis and y-axis labels** are plain language (no variable names like `food_insecure` or question codes like `Q27`).
- [ ] The y-axis label says these are **percents** (e.g., "Percent of respondents").
- [ ] Findings 2 and 3: the **legend** has a plain-language title.
- [ ] The **categories** are in a meaningful order (low to high, or worst to best), not alphabetical.
- [ ] There's **no "NA" bar** or "NA" segment, and no "Refused" or "Don't know" category.
- [ ] The **percent labels** are readable and don't overlap.
- [ ] Someone who has never seen your data could understand the plot **without reading your code**.
:::

1.  **Make a `plots` folder.** [`ggsave()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/32_Data_viz_Design_choices/Data_viz_Design_choices.html#/saving-plots) can't create a folder for you: if the folder doesn't exist, you'll get an error like `Cannot find directory`. In RStudio's **Files** pane, go to your class folder (the one with your `.Rproj` file), click **New Folder**, and name it `plots`.
2.  **Save each plot with `ggsave()`** (Lesson 32). Use [`here()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/12_Rproj_wds/Rproj_wds.html#/the-here-package) to point to your `plots` folder, give each file a descriptive name, and tell `ggsave()` which plot to save:

    ```{r}
    #| eval: false
    ggsave(
      filename = here("plots", "finding1_ease_free_food.png"),
      plot = finding1_plot,
      width = 6, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 300,
      bg = "white"
    )
    ```

    - `bg = "white"` gives the image a white background. Without it, [`theme_minimal()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/32_Data_viz_Design_choices/Data_viz_Design_choices.html#/complete-themes) plots are saved with a see-through background, and the text can disappear on a dark screen or slide.
    - Save at `dpi = 300` or higher so your plot looks crisp on a printed page.
    - Use a descriptive file name for each plot (e.g., `finding1_...`, `finding2_...`) so they're easy to find later.
    - Change `width` and `height` if your labels look crowded. A stacked bar chart with several groups usually needs to be wider.
3.  **Open each `.png` file** from the Files pane and check that it looks the way you expect. The saved image can look different from the plot in RStudio, because the size is different.
4.  Take a screenshot of your `plots` folder showing the files, save it in your `images` folder, and add it to your editing file (the same way you added screenshots in Lab 1).
